name: Mathematics for AI and LLMs
audience: Engineers, architects and technical leaders who want to really understand how models learn and how LLMs compute, and explain it with confidence. High-school algebra assumed; everything else is built up.
format: This site's course with a 40-question practice test mixing concept, calculation and judgment questions.

domains.name: Linear algebra
domains.summary: Vectors, norms, dot products and cosine similarity; matrices as linear maps and shape reasoning for batch x sequence x dimension tensors. Also covers rank, inverses, projections, eigenvalues, SVD, PCA and the low-rank idea behind LoRA, plus broadcasting.

domains.name: Calculus and optimisation
domains.summary: Derivatives, gradients, the chain rule and backpropagation by hand, with Jacobians and Hessians for curvature. Then gradient descent, momentum, Adam and AdamW, weight decay, schedules, saddle points, vanishing and exploding gradients and clipping.

domains.name: Probability and statistics
domains.summary: Random variables, common distributions, expectation and variance, Bayes' theorem with base rates, and maximum likelihood as the reason training minimises negative log-likelihood. Then standard errors, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and A/B tests for model evals.

domains.name: Information theory, losses and decoding
domains.summary: Logits, softmax, sigmoid and stable log-sum-exp; entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence and perplexity. Also covers temperature, top-k, top-p and greedy decoding, plus losses and metrics such as MSE, precision, recall, F1 and calibration.

domains.name: Transformer and LLM mathematics
domains.summary: Embeddings and positional encodings (sinusoidal, RoPE), scaled dot-product and multi-head attention, residuals, normalisation and parameter counting. Then FLOPs per token, Kaplan and Chinchilla scaling, KV-cache memory, and fp16/bf16 and int8/int4 numerics.

scenarios.title: Explaining embeddings and similarity search to a team
scenarios.description: Explain why embeddings are compared by cosine similarity, why normalised vectors make inner product equal cosine, and what dimensionality and low rank mean for a vector store.

scenarios.title: Debugging a training run that diverges
scenarios.description: The loss spikes to NaN. Use gradients, learning rate and curvature, Adam and AdamW settings, clipping and numeric precision to find the cause and fix it.

scenarios.title: Sizing GPU memory for an LLM
scenarios.description: Estimate memory for weights, optimiser state and the KV cache from parameter counts, precision and context length, and decide whether quantisation, GQA or LoRA makes the model fit.

scenarios.title: Reading an ML paper
scenarios.description: Follow the attention equations, loss functions and scaling-law claims in a paper such as Chinchilla, and check its numbers with C ≈ 6ND and simple shape reasoning.

scenarios.title: Designing an eval and judging if a difference is real
scenarios.description: Two models score 71.0% and 71.2%. Use standard errors, confidence intervals, paired tests and multiple-comparison corrections to decide whether the gap is real, and size the eval set beforehand.

lessons.title: Vectors, norms, dot products and cosine similarity
lessons.summary: Why every embedding search, every attention score and every linear layer is, at heart, a dot product, and why embeddings are compared by angle rather than by raw length.

sections.heading: A vector is a point and a direction
sections.body:
An embedding model maps text, an image or a token to a vector $$x\in\mathbb{R}^d$$, a list of $$d$$ real numbers such as 768 or 3072. Read it in two ways at once:

- **Algebraically**, it is an array: `x = np.array([0.12, -0.80, ...])` with shape `(d,)`.
- **Geometrically**, it is an arrow from the origin. The *direction* of the arrow carries meaning ("about refunds", "about Python errors"). The *length* often carries things you do not want to compare on, such as text length, token frequency or how confident the model was.

Most of what follows is a precise way of saying "compare directions, not lengths".

sections.heading: Norms: measuring length
sections.body:
A norm is a length function. The three you will meet:

| Norm | Formula | Use in ML |
|---|---|---|
| L2 (Euclidean) | $$\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\sum_i x_i^2}$$ | default length, weight decay, normalising embeddings |
| L1 | $$\|x\|_1=\sum_i |x_i|$$ | sparsity penalties |
| L∞ | $$\|x\|_\infty=\max_i |x_i|$$ | absmax quantisation scales |

A **unit vector** has $$\|u\|_2=1$$. Normalising means $$u=x/\|x\|_2$$: same direction, length 1.

In NumPy, `np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1, keepdims=True)` gives one norm per row of an `(N, d)` matrix with shape `(N, 1)`, ready to divide `X` by. Dropping `keepdims=True` gives shape `(N,)`, which broadcasts against the *columns*. That is a classic bug, covered in the tensors lesson.

sections.heading: The dot product, two definitions that agree
sections.body:
**Algebraic:** $$a\cdot b=a^\top b=\sum_i a_i b_i$$. This is $$d$$ multiply-adds, which is what GPUs are built for.

**Geometric:** $$a\cdot b=\|a\|\,\|b\|\cos\theta$$, where $$\theta$$ is the angle between the arrows.

Why they agree, in two lines: expand the squared length of the difference vector,
$$\|a-b\|^2=(a-b)\cdot(a-b)=\|a\|^2+\|b\|^2-2\,a\cdot b,$$
and compare with the law of cosines, $$\|a-b\|^2=\|a\|^2+\|b\|^2-2\|a\|\|b\|\cos\theta$$. Matching terms gives the geometric form.

Consequences to keep at your fingertips:

- $$a\cdot b>0$$: the vectors point broadly the same way. $$=0$$: orthogonal. $$<0$$: opposed.
- The **Cauchy–Schwarz inequality** $$|a\cdot b|\le\|a\|\|b\|$$ guarantees that cosine lies in $$[-1,1]$$.
- $$\|a\|^2=a\cdot a$$, so the norm is just the dot product of a vector with itself.

sections.heading: Cosine similarity and why embeddings use it
sections.body:
$$\cos(a,b)=\frac{a\cdot b}{\|a\|\,\|b\|}$$

It is the dot product with the lengths divided out, so it depends **only on the angle**. Worked examples (verified in NumPy):

- $$a=(1,2,3)$$, $$b=(2,4,6)$$: $$a\cdot b=28$$, $$\|a\|=\sqrt{14}\approx3.742$$, $$\|b\|=2\sqrt{14}$$, so cos = 1.0. The vectors are parallel; $$b$$ is just longer.
- $$a=(1,2,3)$$, $$c=(3,-1,0)$$: $$a\cdot c=3-2+0=1$$, so cos $$=1/\sqrt{140}\approx0.0845$$, nearly orthogonal.

**Why it fits embeddings.** If two passages say the same thing but one vector is longer, a raw dot product would favour the longer vector for *every* query. Cosine removes that bias.

**The production trick.** Normalise every vector once at index time. For unit vectors, $$u\cdot v=\cos(u,v)$$, so the database can run a plain inner-product search, which is a single matrix multiply.

**Euclidean distance agrees on unit vectors.** From the expansion above with $$\|u\|=\|v\|=1$$:
$$\|u-v\|^2=2-2\cos(u,v).$$
Smaller distance means larger cosine, so the nearest-neighbour *ranking* is identical. Only the score scale differs.

sections.heading: Python: similarity for a whole batch at once
sections.body:
Never loop over pairs in Python. With queries `Q` of shape `(N, d)` and documents `Dm` of shape `(M, d)`:

```python
import numpy as np

def l2_normalize(X, eps=1e-12):
    return X / np.maximum(np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1, keepdims=True), eps)

Qn, Dn = l2_normalize(Q), l2_normalize(Dm)
S = Qn @ Dn.T                 # (N, d) @ (d, M) -> (N, M) cosine matrix
top5 = np.argsort(-S, axis=1)[:, :5]   # best 5 documents per query
```

`S[i, j]` is the cosine between query `i` and document `j`. The `eps` guard stops a zero vector from producing `nan`. Attention does the same thing: $$QK^\top$$ is a matrix of dot products between every query and every key, before scaling and softmax.

keyPoints: $$a\cdot b=\sum_i a_ib_i=\|a\|\|b\|\cos\theta$$; the two forms agree by the law of cosines.
Cosine similarity divides out length, so it compares direction only and lies in $$[-1,1]$$.
Normalise once, then inner product equals cosine; vector stores rely on this.
For unit vectors $$\|u-v\|^2=2-2\cos$$, so Euclidean and cosine give the same ranking.
A batch of similarities is one matrix multiply: normalised queries times normalised documents transposed.

gotchas.trap: Using a raw inner-product index on embeddings that were never normalised.
gotchas.correct: Normalise at write time and at query time, or use a cosine metric; otherwise long vectors win every query.

gotchas.trap: Believing cosine and Euclidean search can return different neighbours on normalised vectors.
gotchas.correct: On unit vectors $$\|u-v\|^2=2-2\cos$$, so the order of neighbours is the same.

gotchas.trap: Dividing by `np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1)` without `keepdims=True`.
gotchas.correct: Keep the axis so the shape is `(N, 1)` and each row is divided by its own norm.

lessons.lab:
1. In NumPy compute the cosine of $$(1,2,3)$$ with $$(2,4,6)$$ and with $$(3,-1,0)$$. Expect 1.0 and about 0.0845.
2. Generate 1,000 random 768-dim vectors, normalise them and form the Gram matrix `E @ E.T`. Check that the diagonal is all 1 and that off-diagonal cosines cluster near 0: random high-dimensional directions are nearly orthogonal.
3. Verify $$\|u-v\|^2=2-2\,u\cdot v$$ numerically for two unit vectors.

lessons.title: Matrices as linear maps and shape reasoning
lessons.summary: A matrix is a function that moves vectors. Matrix multiplication is function composition, and every bug in a model forward pass starts as a shape you did not reason about.

sections.heading: What "linear" means
sections.body:
A map $$f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$$ is linear when $$f(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha f(x)+\beta f(y)$$. Every such map is a matrix $$A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$$ with $$f(x)=Ax$$, and the **columns of $$A$$ are where the basis vectors land**: column $$j$$ is $$Ae_j$$.

That one sentence lets you read any matrix. A $$2\times2$$ rotation by 90° is $$\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$$ because it sends $$e_1=(1,0)$$ to $$(0,1)$$ and $$e_2$$ to $$(-1,0)$$.

Each output entry is a dot product: $$(Ax)_i=\text{row}_i(A)\cdot x$$. So a linear layer computes "how much does the input align with each learned row direction".

sections.heading: Matrix multiplication is composition
sections.body:
$$(AB)x=A(Bx)$$: apply $$B$$ first, then $$A$$. The entry formula follows:
$$C=AB,\qquad C_{ij}=\sum_k A_{ik}B_{kj}.$$

Rules that fall out of this:

- **Inner dimensions must match**: $$(m\times n)(n\times p)\to(m\times p)$$.
- **Not commutative.** With $$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}$$ and the swap $$B=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$$, $$AB$$ swaps the *columns* of $$A$$ while $$BA$$ swaps its *rows*: $$AB=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\4&3\end{bmatrix}$$, $$BA=\begin{bmatrix}3&4\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$$.
- **Associative**: $$(AB)C=A(BC)$$, but the cost can differ a lot, so the order of evaluation matters for speed.
- **Cost**: $$m\cdot n\cdot p$$ multiply-adds, roughly $$2mnp$$ floating-point operations. This is where "about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token" for a forward pass comes from.
- Stacking linear maps without a nonlinearity gives **another single linear map**. That is why networks put activations between layers.

sections.heading: nn.Linear, written out
sections.body:
PyTorch's `nn.Linear(in_features, out_features)` computes $$y=xW^\top+b$$ and stores `weight` with shape `(out_features, in_features)`. The input can have any leading dimensions; only the last one must equal `in_features`.

Parameter count = $$\text{in}\times\text{out}+\text{out}$$ (with bias). For a transformer MLP up-projection `nn.Linear(768, 3072)`: $$768\cdot3072+3072=2{,}362{,}368$$ parameters, and `weight.shape == (3072, 768)` (verified on PyTorch 2.8).

The transpose in $$xW^\top$$ is a storage convention: each *row* of `weight` is one output neuron's direction, so $$y_j=x\cdot W_j+b_j$$.

sections.heading: Shape reasoning: batch × seq × dim
sections.body:
Language models carry activations of shape `(B, T, D)`: batch, sequence length, model width. Learn to read every operation as a shape transformation.

| Step | Shapes | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Token embeddings | ids `(B, T)` indexing a table `(V, D)` | `(B, T, D)` |
| Linear projection | `(B, T, D) @ (D, D')` | `(B, T, D')` |
| Split heads | reshape to `(B, T, h, d)`, then transpose | `(B, h, T, d)`, with $$D=h\cdot d$$ |
| Attention scores | `Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1)`: `(B, h, T, d) @ (B, h, d, T)` | `(B, h, T, T)` |
| Weighted values | `softmax(scores) @ V` | `(B, h, T, d)` |

Key facts:

- `@` / `matmul` on tensors with more than 2 dims treats the **last two** as the matrix and the rest as a **batch** that broadcasts. `(2, 5, 8) @ (8, 16)` gives `(2, 5, 16)`; `(4, 1, 5, 8) @ (3, 8, 2)` gives `(4, 3, 5, 2)` (both verified).
- A linear layer on `(B, T, D)` acts on every token independently with the **same** weights. Mixing *across* tokens only happens in attention, through the `(T, T)` score matrix.
- The `(T, T)` scores are why attention costs grow with the square of sequence length.

sections.heading: Habits that prevent shape bugs
sections.body:
- Write the shape next to every tensor in comments: `# (B, h, T, d)`.
- Assert shapes at module boundaries: `assert x.shape[-1] == self.d_model`.
- Name the contracted dimension: in `Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1)` the shared `d` disappears and two `T` axes remain.
- Use `einsum` when the shape story matters more than the call: `np.einsum('bhqd,bhkd->bhqk', Q, K)` states the contraction explicitly.
- Prefer `transpose(-2, -1)` over `.T` on batched tensors: `.T` reverses *all* axes.

keyPoints: The columns of a matrix are the images of the basis vectors.
$$AB$$ means apply $$B$$ then $$A$$; inner dimensions must match; order matters.
`nn.Linear(in, out)` computes $$xW^\top+b$$ with weight shape `(out, in)` and in·out+out parameters.
Batched matmul uses the last two dims as the matrix and broadcasts the leading ones.
Attention scores have shape (B, h, T, T): this is the source of quadratic cost in sequence length.

gotchas.trap: Assuming `nn.Linear(768, 3072).weight` has shape (768, 3072).
gotchas.correct: It is (out, in) = (3072, 768); the layer computes $$xW^\top+b$$.

gotchas.trap: Writing `K.T` on a 4-D key tensor to get $$K^\top$$ for attention.
gotchas.correct: Use `K.transpose(-2, -1)` to swap only the sequence and head-dim axes.

gotchas.trap: Stacking linear layers without activations to add capacity.
gotchas.correct: A product of matrices is one matrix; without a nonlinearity the stack is still a single linear map.

lessons.lab:
1. Build `nn.Linear(768, 3072)` and print `weight.shape` and the total parameter count. Expect (3072, 768) and 2,362,368.
2. Create `Q, K, V` of shape `(2, 8, 10, 64)` and compute `softmax(Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) / 8, dim=-1) @ V`. Predict every intermediate shape before printing it.
3. Show that `A @ B != B @ A` for the matrices in this lesson, and that `(A @ B).T == B.T @ A.T`.

lessons.title: Transpose, inverse, rank, independence and projections
lessons.summary: The vocabulary that tells you when a system has a unique answer, when information has been lost, and how least squares finds the closest answer when no exact one exists.

sections.heading: Transpose
sections.body:
$$(A^\top)_{ij}=A_{ji}$$: rows become columns. The rules you use daily:

- $$(AB)^\top=B^\top A^\top$$ (the order reverses, just like taking off socks and shoes).
- $$a\cdot b=a^\top b$$, so $$x^\top A y$$ is a scalar "bilinear" score; attention's $$q^\top k$$ is the special case $$A=I$$.
- A matrix is **symmetric** when $$A=A^\top$$. Covariance matrices and Gram matrices $$X^\top X$$ are always symmetric, which buys them real eigenvalues (next lesson).

sections.heading: Linear independence, span and rank
sections.body:
Vectors $$v_1,\dots,v_k$$ are **linearly independent** if no one of them is a combination of the others, equivalently $$\sum c_iv_i=0$$ only when all $$c_i=0$$.

The **rank** of $$A$$ is the number of independent columns, which always equals the number of independent rows. It is the dimension of the column space: the set of all outputs $$Ax$$ can reach.

- $$\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}$$ has rank 1 (`np.linalg.matrix_rank` confirms): column 2 is twice column 1, so every output lies on one line. Its determinant is 0.
- $$\operatorname{rank}(A)\le\min(m,n)$$, and $$\operatorname{rank}(AB)\le\min(\operatorname{rank}A,\operatorname{rank}B)$$. A product that passes through a narrow $$r$$-dimensional bottleneck has rank at most $$r$$, which is exactly the LoRA idea.
- Numerically, rank is the number of singular values above a tolerance, which is how `matrix_rank` computes it.

A rank-deficient map **loses information**: different inputs collapse to the same output (the null space is non-trivial), so it cannot be undone.

sections.heading: Inverse, and why you rarely compute it
sections.body:
A square $$A$$ is invertible iff it has full rank (equivalently $$\det A\ne0$$, equivalently its null space is just $$\{0\}$$). Then $$A^{-1}A=I$$ and $$(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$$.

**Orthogonal matrices** are the friendliest case: $$Q^\top Q=I$$, so $$Q^{-1}=Q^\top$$. They preserve lengths and dot products ($$\|Qx\|=\|x\|$$, $$(Qx)\cdot(Qy)=x\cdot y$$). Rotations are orthogonal; RoPE rotates query and key pairs so that their dot product depends only on the relative position.

**In code, solve instead of invert.** To get $$x$$ from $$Ax=b$$, call `np.linalg.solve(A, b)`, not `np.linalg.inv(A) @ b`. Solving is cheaper and more accurate. When $$A$$ is ill-conditioned (largest/smallest singular value is huge) results lose digits either way; the NumPy docs suggest checking `np.linalg.cond`. A condition number of $$10^k$$ can cost up to about $$k$$ digits.

sections.heading: Projections and least squares
sections.body:
The projection of $$v$$ onto the line through $$u$$ is
$$\operatorname{proj}_u v=\frac{v\cdot u}{u\cdot u}\,u.$$
*Derivation:* look for $$\hat v=c\,u$$ whose residual $$v-cu$$ is orthogonal to $$u$$: $$(v-cu)\cdot u=0\Rightarrow c=\frac{v\cdot u}{u\cdot u}$$.

Example: $$v=(3,1)$$, $$u=(1,1)$$: $$c=4/2=2$$, so $$\hat v=(2,2)$$ and the residual $$(1,-1)$$ is perpendicular to $$u$$.

**Onto a subspace.** For the column space of $$A$$ (full column rank), the same orthogonality condition $$A^\top(b-A\hat x)=0$$ gives the **normal equations**
$$A^\top A\,\hat x=A^\top b,\qquad P=A(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top.$$
This is least squares, i.e. linear regression: the best fit is the projection of the targets onto the span of the features. A projection matrix satisfies $$P^2=P$$ (projecting twice changes nothing).

Example: fit $$y=c_0+c_1t$$ to points $$(0,1),(1,2),(2,2)$$. `np.linalg.lstsq`, the normal equations and `np.linalg.pinv(A) @ b` all give $$c_0=7/6$$, $$c_1=1/2$$. In practice prefer `lstsq`, which works through the SVD and also handles rank-deficient $$A$$ via the pseudoinverse.

keyPoints: $$(AB)^\top=B^\top A^\top$$ and $$(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$$: both reverse the order.
Rank = number of independent columns = dimension of the reachable outputs = number of non-zero singular values.
Square and full rank $$\Leftrightarrow$$ invertible $$\Leftrightarrow$$ $$\det\ne0$$.
Orthogonal matrices: $$Q^{-1}=Q^\top$$; they preserve lengths and dot products.
Projection: residual is orthogonal to the subspace; least squares solves $$A^\top A\hat x=A^\top b$$.

gotchas.trap: Writing `np.linalg.inv(A) @ b` to solve a linear system.
gotchas.correct: Use `np.linalg.solve(A, b)` (or `lstsq` for non-square or rank-deficient systems).

gotchas.trap: Assuming a 1000×1000 matrix has rank 1000 because of its size.
gotchas.correct: Rank is about independence; a product $$BA$$ with inner size $$r$$ has rank at most $$r$$ whatever its outer size.

gotchas.trap: Expecting $$(AB)^\top=A^\top B^\top$$.
gotchas.correct: The order reverses: $$(AB)^\top=B^\top A^\top$$.

lessons.lab:
1. Check `np.linalg.matrix_rank([[1,2],[2,4]])` (expect 1) and that `np.linalg.det` is 0.
2. Project $$(3,1)$$ onto $$(1,1)$$ by the formula and confirm the residual is orthogonal.
3. Fit a line to $$(0,1),(1,2),(2,2)$$ with `lstsq`, normal equations and `pinv`. All three should give $$(7/6,\ 1/2)$$.
4. Build a 90° rotation $$Q$$ and verify `Q.T @ Q` is the identity and that $$\|Qx\|=\|x\|$$.

lessons.title: Eigenvectors, SVD, PCA and why LoRA works
lessons.summary: Decompositions reveal the few directions that matter. The SVD gives the best low-rank approximation of any matrix, PCA is the SVD of centred data, and LoRA bets that fine-tuning updates are low-rank.

sections.heading: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
sections.body:
An eigenvector of a square $$A$$ is a direction the map only stretches: $$Av=\lambda v$$, with eigenvalue $$\lambda$$.

**Symmetric matrices** (the spectral theorem): all eigenvalues are real and the eigenvectors can be chosen orthonormal, so $$A=Q\Lambda Q^\top$$. In words: rotate into the eigenbasis, scale each axis, rotate back.

Example: $$A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$$. $$A(1,1)^\top=(3,3)^\top$$ and $$A(1,-1)^\top=(1,-1)^\top$$, so the eigenvalues are 3 and 1 with eigenvectors along $$(1,1)$$ and $$(1,-1)$$. `np.linalg.eigvalsh` returns them as `[1., 3.]`: **ascending** order.

Why ML cares:
- A covariance matrix is symmetric positive semi-definite, so its eigenvalues are $$\ge0$$ and equal the variance along each eigenvector.
- Eigenvalues of a Hessian measure curvature per direction; a large ratio means an ill-conditioned problem for gradient descent.
- Repeatedly applying $$A$$ amplifies the top-eigenvalue direction, the linear-algebra root of exploding and vanishing signals.

sections.heading: The SVD: every matrix is rotate, scale, rotate
sections.body:
Any real $$A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$$, square or not, factors as
$$A=U\Sigma V^\top=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_i\,u_i v_i^\top,$$
with orthonormal columns in $$U$$ and $$V$$ and singular values $$\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\dots\ge0$$.

- $$\sigma_i^2$$ are the eigenvalues of $$A^\top A$$; $$v_i$$ are its eigenvectors.
- Rank = number of non-zero $$\sigma_i$$.
- The sum form shows $$A$$ as a weighted stack of **rank-1** pieces, ordered by importance.

NumPy details: `np.linalg.svd` returns `U, S, Vh` with `S` in **descending** order and `Vh` already transposed. By default `full_matrices=True`, so for a `(6, 4)` input `U` is `(6, 6)`; pass `full_matrices=False` for the compact `(6, 4)` version.

sections.heading: Eckart–Young: the best low-rank approximation
sections.body:
Keep the top $$k$$ terms: $$A_k=\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_iu_iv_i^\top$$. The Eckart–Young theorem says no rank-$$k$$ matrix is closer to $$A$$, in either norm:
$$\|A-A_k\|_2=\sigma_{k+1},\qquad \|A-A_k\|_F=\sqrt{\textstyle\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2}.$$

Worked example (`rng = np.random.default_rng(0); A = rng.standard_normal((6, 4))`): $$\sigma=(3.0361,\,2.0335,\,1.8563,\,0.8954)$$.
- Rank 1: spectral error $$\sigma_2=2.0335$$; Frobenius error $$\sqrt{2.0335^2+1.8563^2+0.8954^2}\approx2.8953$$.
- Rank 2: spectral error $$\sigma_3=1.8563$$; Frobenius error $$\sqrt{1.8563^2+0.8954^2}\approx2.0610$$.
- Energy kept by rank 2: $$(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)/\sum\sigma_i^2\approx0.76$$.

A random Gaussian matrix has a *flat* spectrum, so truncation hurts. Real weight updates and real data often have a fast-decaying spectrum, so a small $$k$$ keeps almost everything.

sections.heading: PCA is the SVD of centred data
sections.body:
Given data $$X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$$:
1. Centre: subtract the column means (scikit-learn's `PCA` does this for you; it does not scale features).
2. SVD: $$X_c=U\Sigma V^\top$$. The rows of $$V^\top$$ are the principal directions (`components_`).
3. Variance along component $$i$$ is $$\sigma_i^2/(n-1)$$; `explained_variance_ratio_` is each share of the total.
4. Project: $$Z=X_cV_k$$ gives $$k$$-dimensional coordinates.

Equivalently, the components are eigenvectors of the covariance $$\frac{1}{n-1}X_c^\top X_c$$. Without centring, the first "component" mostly points at the mean, not along the spread.

Example: 200 samples of 3-D Gaussian noise scaled by $$(3,1,0.1)$$ give explained variance ratios of about $$[0.902,0.097,0.001]$$: two components carry 99.9% of the variance. This is how you visualise embeddings in 2-D, and why compressing embeddings to fewer dimensions can lose little.

sections.heading: Why LoRA works
sections.body:
Full fine-tuning learns an update $$\Delta W$$ the size of $$W_0\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}$$. LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) freezes $$W_0$$ and constrains the update to a product of two thin matrices:
$$h=W_0x+\Delta Wx=W_0x+BAx,\qquad B\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r},\ A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times k},\ r\ll\min(d,k).$$

- **Rank budget.** $$\operatorname{rank}(BA)\le r$$: the update can only move the layer's outputs within an $$r$$-dimensional subspace.
- **Parameter count.** $$r(d+k)$$ instead of $$dk$$. For $$d=k=4096$$, $$r=8$$: 65,536 vs 16,777,216, 256× fewer for that matrix.
- **Initialisation.** $$A$$ is random Gaussian and $$B$$ is zero, so $$\Delta W=BA=0$$ at step 0 and the adapted model starts exactly at the pretrained one.
- **Scaling.** The update is scaled by $$\alpha/r$$, which reduces the need to retune the learning rate when $$r$$ changes.
- **No inference latency.** After training, merge $$W=W_0+\frac{\alpha}{r}BA$$; the deployed layer is a single matrix again.
- **The hypothesis.** The paper argues that weight *updates* during adaptation have a low "intrinsic rank", which Eckart–Young says can be captured well by a rank-$$r$$ factorisation. Their experiments mostly adapt $$W_q$$ and $$W_v$$, and found even very small $$r$$ competitive. On GPT-3 175B they report about 10,000× fewer trainable parameters and about 3× less GPU memory than full fine-tuning.

keyPoints: Symmetric $$\Rightarrow$$ real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors: $$A=Q\Lambda Q^\top$$.
SVD exists for every matrix: $$A=U\Sigma V^\top=\sum\sigma_iu_iv_i^\top$$; rank = number of non-zero $$\sigma_i$$.
Truncated SVD is the best rank-$$k$$ approximation; spectral error $$\sigma_{k+1}$$, Frobenius error $$\sqrt{\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2}$$.
PCA = centre, then SVD; components are right singular vectors / covariance eigenvectors.
LoRA: $$\Delta W=BA$$, rank $$\le r$$, $$B=0$$ at init, scaled by $$\alpha/r$$, mergeable for zero added latency.
`eigvalsh` returns ascending eigenvalues; `svd` returns descending singular values.

gotchas.trap: Taking `eigvalsh(C)[0]` as the largest eigenvalue of a covariance matrix.
gotchas.correct: It is the smallest; `eigvalsh` sorts ascending. Use `[-1]`, or SVD whose values are descending.

gotchas.trap: Running PCA on uncentred data by hand.
gotchas.correct: Subtract the column means first; scikit-learn PCA centres automatically.

gotchas.trap: Initialising both LoRA matrices randomly.
gotchas.correct: Keep $$B=0$$ (or otherwise $$BA=0$$) so training starts from the pretrained function.

gotchas.trap: Assuming LoRA adds inference latency.
gotchas.correct: $$BA$$ can be merged into $$W_0$$, so the served model has the original shapes.

lessons.lab:

2. With `A = np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal((6, 4))`, build rank-1 and rank-2 truncations and check the error formulas against `np.linalg.norm(A - Ak, 'fro')` and `np.linalg.norm(A - Ak, 2)`.
3. Fit `sklearn.decomposition.PCA` to data scaled by $$(3,1,0.1)$$ and read `explained_variance_ratio_`.
4. Count LoRA parameters for $$d=4096$$, $$k=11008$$, $$r=16$$: $$16\cdot(4096+11008)=241{,}664$$ vs 45,088,768 for the full matrix.

lessons.title: Tensors and broadcasting, the language of deep learning
lessons.summary: Deep-learning code is written in whole-tensor operations. Broadcasting rules decide which of those operations are legal and, more dangerously, which illegal-looking ones silently succeed.

sections.heading: Tensors: shape, dtype, device, and named axes
sections.body:
A tensor is an n-dimensional array: a scalar (0-D), vector (1-D), matrix (2-D), or more. What matters in practice is its **shape** and what each axis *means*:

- Text model activations: `(B, T, D)` = batch, tokens, features.
- Multi-head attention: `(B, h, T, d)` with $$D=h\cdot d$$.
- Images: `(B, C, H, W)` in PyTorch.

Reductions take an `axis`/`dim` and remove it unless you pass `keepdims=True` / `keepdim=True`. Mean-pooling a sequence is `x.mean(dim=1)`: `(B, T, D)` to `(B, D)`.

sections.heading: The broadcasting rules
sections.body:
When two arrays of different shapes meet in an element-wise operation, NumPy and PyTorch compare shapes **from the trailing (rightmost) dimension leftward**. Two dimensions are compatible when

1. they are equal, or
2. one of them is 1.

A missing leading dimension is treated as 1. Each size-1 dimension is (virtually) stretched to match; nothing is copied in memory.

| A | B | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `(3, 1)` | `(1, 4)` | `(3, 4)` |
| `(5, 4)` | `(4,)` | `(5, 4)` (per-column bias) |
| `(5, 4)` | `(5,)` | error: trailing 4 vs 5 |
| `(15, 3, 5)` | `(3, 1)` | `(15, 3, 5)` |
| `(8, 1, 6, 1)` | `(7, 1, 5)` | `(8, 7, 6, 5)` |

All rows were checked with `np.broadcast_shapes`. Adding a bias `b` of shape `(D,)` to `(B, T, D)` works because `(D,)` aligns with the last axis.

sections.heading: Silent broadcasting bugs
sections.body:
Broadcasting errors are loud. Broadcasting *successes* you did not intend are the real danger.

**1. The (N,) minus (N, 1) trap.** `y` has shape `(N,)` and `pred` has shape `(N, 1)`. `y - pred` broadcasts to `(N, N)`: every target minus every prediction. `((y - pred)**2).mean()` runs, returns a number, and is wrong. Fix with `pred.squeeze(-1)` or `y[:, None]`.

**2. Row normalisation without keepdims.** `X / np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1)` divides `(N, D)` by `(N,)`. It errors when $$N\ne D$$, but when the matrix happens to be square it silently divides *columns* by row norms. Always `keepdims=True`.

**3. Masked mean-pooling.** Hidden states `(B, T, D)` times an attention mask `(B, T)` fails (trailing `D` vs `T`). The fix is `mask[..., None]` to make `(B, T, 1)`:

```python
m = mask[..., None].to(h.dtype)          # (B, T, 1)
pooled = (h * m).sum(1) / m.sum(1)       # (B, D) / (B, 1) -> (B, D)
```

**Defence:** assert shapes after any operation that mixes tensors of different rank.

sections.heading: Reshape, view, transpose and einsum
sections.body:
Splitting heads is the canonical sequence:

```python
x = x.view(B, T, h, d).transpose(1, 2)   # (B, T, D) -> (B, h, T, d)
# ... attention ...
x = x.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, D)   # back to (B, T, D)
```

- `transpose` only swaps axes in the metadata (strides); the result is usually **non-contiguous**.
- `view` needs compatible strides and raises an error on many non-contiguous tensors. `reshape` returns a view when it can and copies when it must. That is why the merge step uses `reshape` (or `.contiguous().view(...)`).
- Reshaping `(B, T, D)` straight to `(B, h, T, d)` without the transpose is legal but **scrambles** tokens and features: the numbers end up in the wrong axes.

**einsum** writes the contraction explicitly: `np.einsum('qd,kd->qk', Q, K)` equals `Q @ K.T`. Letters on both inputs but not the output are summed over; letters that survive define the output shape.

keyPoints: Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right; each pair must be equal or contain a 1.
Size-1 axes stretch virtually; no memory is copied.
(N,) combined with (N, 1) yields (N, N): the most common silent bug.
Use keepdims=True for per-row reductions you will divide or subtract with.
transpose makes tensors non-contiguous; view may then fail, reshape will copy if needed.
einsum labels make contractions explicit and readable.

gotchas.trap: Computing an MSE between targets of shape (N,) and predictions of shape (N, 1).
gotchas.correct: Squeeze or unsqueeze so both have the same shape; otherwise the loss is averaged over an (N, N) matrix.

gotchas.trap: Multiplying hidden states (B, T, D) by a mask (B, T) directly.
gotchas.correct: Add a trailing axis: `mask[..., None]` gives (B, T, 1).

gotchas.trap: Reshaping (B, T, D) directly to (B, h, T, d) to split heads.
gotchas.correct: Reshape to (B, T, h, d) first, then transpose(1, 2).

lessons.lab:
1. Predict, then check with `np.broadcast_shapes`: `(8,1,6,1)` with `(7,1,5)`; `(5,4)` with `(5,)`.
2. Reproduce the `(N,) - (N,1)` bug with `N = 5` and print the result shape.
3. In PyTorch, split a `(2, 10, 512)` tensor into 8 heads, then call `.view(2, 8, 640)` on the transposed tensor and read the error. Fix it with `reshape`.
4. Implement masked mean-pooling and confirm padded positions do not affect the result.

lessons.title: Derivatives, partial derivatives and gradients
lessons.summary: The derivative as the best local linear model, partial derivatives, the gradient vector, directional derivatives and why the negative gradient is the steepest way down. Ends with checking gradients numerically in Python.

sections.heading: The derivative is a local linear model
sections.body:
The single most useful way to read a derivative is as the slope of the best straight-line approximation near a point:

$$f(x+h)\approx f(x)+f'(x)\,h\quad\text{for small }h$$

with $$f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$$. Everything in optimisation is built on this idea: if you know the slope you know which way to nudge $$x$$ to make $$f$$ smaller, and roughly how much it will drop.

Derivatives you should be able to write without thinking, because they appear in every network:

| Function | Derivative | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| $$x^n$$ | $$n x^{n-1}$$ | squared-error losses |
| $$e^x$$ | $$e^x$$ | softmax, exp in attention |
| $$\ln x$$ | $$1/x$$ | log-likelihood, cross-entropy |
| $$\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}$$ | $$\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x))$$ | max value 0.25 at $$x=0$$, the root of vanishing gradients |
| $$\tanh x$$ | $$1-\tanh^2 x$$ | max value 1 at $$x=0$$ |
| $$\mathrm{ReLU}(x)=\max(0,x)$$ | 1 if $$x>0$$, 0 if $$x<0$$ | not differentiable at 0; frameworks pick a convention |

Plus the product rule $$(uv)'=u'v+uv'$$ and the chain rule (next lesson).

sections.heading: Partial derivatives and the gradient
sections.body:
A loss depends on many parameters. A **partial derivative** $$\partial f/\partial x_i$$ is the ordinary derivative with respect to one coordinate while all the others are held fixed. Stack them and you get the **gradient**:

$$\nabla f(x)=\Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1},\dots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}\Big)$$

The multivariable version of the linear model is

$$f(x+\delta)\approx f(x)+\nabla f(x)\cdot\delta$$

**Worked example.** Take $$f(x,y)=x^2+3y^2$$. Then $$\partial f/\partial x=2x$$ and $$\partial f/\partial y=6y$$, so at $$(1,1)$$ the gradient is $$(2,6)$$.

**Shape rule for code.** The gradient of a scalar loss with respect to a tensor has the *same shape as that tensor*. In PyTorch, `p.grad` always has `p.shape`. If you ever compute a gradient whose shape differs from the parameter, you made a mistake.

sections.heading: Directional derivatives and steepest descent
sections.body:
How fast does $$f$$ change if you move in direction $$u$$? For a **unit** vector $$u$$:

$$D_u f(x)=\nabla f(x)\cdot u=\|\nabla f(x)\|\cos\theta$$

where $$\theta$$ is the angle between $$u$$ and the gradient. Three consequences follow straight from $$\cos\theta$$:

1. $$\theta=0$$: moving along $$\nabla f$$ gives the **largest** increase, at rate $$\|\nabla f\|$$.
2. $$\theta=180^\circ$$: moving along $$-\nabla f$$ gives the **steepest decrease**. This is why gradient descent steps along the negative gradient.
3. $$\theta=90^\circ$$: moving perpendicular to the gradient leaves $$f$$ unchanged to first order. The gradient is perpendicular to level sets (contour lines).

**Worked example.** At $$(1,1)$$ for $$f=x^2+3y^2$$, $$\nabla f=(2,6)$$ and $$\|\nabla f\|=\sqrt{40}\approx6.32$$. In the direction of $$(3,4)$$ you must first normalise: $$u=(0.6,0.8)$$, so $$D_uf=2(0.6)+6(0.8)=6.0$$. Forgetting to normalise gives 30, which is wrong by the factor $$\|(3,4)\|=5$$.

Note that the steepest-descent direction $$-(2,6)/\sqrt{40}$$ does **not** point at the minimum $$(0,0)$$. On a stretched bowl the gradient points across the valley, not along it. That mismatch is the seed of the zig-zag behaviour you will meet in the curvature lesson.

sections.heading: Checking a gradient numerically
sections.body:
When you derive a gradient by hand, check it against finite differences:

- Forward difference: $$\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$$, error $$O(h)$$.
- Central difference: $$\frac{f(x+h)-f(x-h)}{2h}$$, error $$O(h^2)$$.

For $$f=x^3$$ at $$x=2$$ (true value 12) with $$h=10^{-3}$$, forward gives 12.006001 and central gives 12.000001. The central formula is about three orders of magnitude more accurate for the same $$h$$.

Do not shrink $$h$$ without limit: subtracting two nearly equal floats loses digits (catastrophic cancellation), so very small $$h$$ makes things *worse*, especially in float32. Do checks in float64. PyTorch ships `torch.autograd.gradcheck`, which compares analytical gradients with finite differences for you.

```python
import torch
x = torch.tensor([1.0, 1.0], requires_grad=True)
f = x[0]**2 + 3 * x[1]**2
f.backward()
print(x.grad)                         # tensor([2., 6.])
u = torch.tensor([3.0, 4.0]); u = u / u.norm()
print((x.grad @ u).item())            # 6.0  directional derivative
```

keyPoints: A derivative is the slope of the best local linear model: f(x+h) ≈ f(x) + f'(x)h.
The gradient stacks the partial derivatives and has the same shape as the parameters.
Directional derivative along a unit vector u is ∇f·u = ‖∇f‖cosθ; normalise u first.
The negative gradient is the direction of steepest local decrease, but it need not point at the minimum.
Central differences have O(h²) error versus O(h) for forward differences; check gradients in float64.
σ'(x) = σ(x)(1−σ(x)) peaks at 0.25, which is why stacked sigmoids shrink gradients.

gotchas.trap: Computing a directional derivative with an unnormalised direction vector.
gotchas.correct: Divide by the vector's norm first; otherwise the result is scaled by that norm.

gotchas.trap: Assuming the steepest-descent direction points straight at the minimum.
gotchas.correct: It is perpendicular to the contour line through the current point; on an elongated bowl it points across the valley.

gotchas.trap: Making the finite-difference step h as small as possible for accuracy.
gotchas.correct: Below a point, round-off from subtracting nearly equal numbers dominates; use a moderate h, central differences and float64.

lessons.lab:
1. In Python, define `f = lambda x, y: x**2 + 3*y**2` and compute the gradient at (1, 1) by hand, then with PyTorch autograd.
2. Compute the directional derivative toward (3, 4) both correctly (normalised) and incorrectly (raw), and explain the factor of 5.
3. Implement forward and central differences for `x**3` at 2 with h in [1e-1, 1e-3, 1e-5, 1e-8, 1e-12] in float64 and float32. Plot or print the absolute error and find where round-off takes over.
4. Run `torch.autograd.gradcheck` on a small function of a float64 tensor and confirm it returns True.

lessons.title: Chain rule, computational graphs and backprop by hand
lessons.summary: Derive gradients through composed functions, see backpropagation as the chain rule applied in reverse over a graph, work a tiny network by hand, and learn the autograd behaviours that cause real bugs.

sections.heading: The chain rule
sections.body:
If $$y=g(u)$$ and $$u=h(x)$$, then

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy}{du}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}$$

**Worked example.** $$y=(3x^2+1)^2$$ at $$x=2$$. Let $$u=3x^2+1=13$$, so $$y=169$$. Then $$dy/du=2u=26$$ and $$du/dx=6x=12$$, giving $$dy/dx=26\times12=312$$. Autograd returns exactly 312.

**Multivariable chain rule.** If $$x$$ influences $$y$$ through several intermediate variables $$u_1,\dots,u_k$$, you sum over the paths:

$$\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}=\sum_j\frac{\partial y}{\partial u_j}\frac{\partial u_j}{\partial x}$$

This "sum over paths" is why, in a computational graph, gradients arriving at a node that fans out to several consumers are **added**.

sections.heading: Computational graphs: forward caches, backward multiplies
sections.body:
Write the computation as a graph of primitive operations. Training then has two passes:

- **Forward pass.** Evaluate the nodes in order and **cache** the intermediate values that the local derivatives will need (for example the pre-activation of each ReLU).
- **Backward pass.** Start from $$\partial L/\partial L=1$$ and visit nodes in reverse order. Each node multiplies the incoming upstream gradient by its local derivative and passes the result to its inputs. Where a value was used twice, its gradients add.

Two practical consequences:

1. **Activation memory.** The cached intermediates are why training needs much more memory than inference, and why techniques such as activation checkpointing trade recomputation for memory.
2. **Reverse mode is cheap for scalar losses.** One backward pass yields the gradient with respect to *every* parameter at a cost that is a small constant multiple of the forward pass. Forward-mode differentiation would need one pass per input direction, which is hopeless with billions of parameters.

sections.heading: Backprop by hand on a tiny network
sections.body:
Model: $$z=w_1x+b_1$$, $$h=\mathrm{ReLU}(z)$$, $$\hat y=w_2h$$, $$L=(\hat y-y)^2$$.
Values: $$x=1$$, $$w_1=2$$, $$b_1=-0.5$$, $$w_2=3$$, $$y=2$$.

**Forward:** $$z=1.5$$, $$h=1.5$$, $$\hat y=4.5$$, $$L=2.5^2=6.25$$.

**Backward** (each line = upstream gradient × local derivative):

| Quantity | Computation | Value |
|---|---|---|
| $$\partial L/\partial\hat y$$ | $$2(\hat y-y)$$ | 5 |
| $$\partial L/\partial w_2$$ | $$5\cdot h$$ | 7.5 |
| $$\partial L/\partial h$$ | $$5\cdot w_2$$ | 15 |
| $$\partial L/\partial z$$ | $$15\cdot\mathrm{ReLU}'(1.5)=15\cdot1$$ | 15 |
| $$\partial L/\partial w_1$$ | $$15\cdot x$$ | 15 |
| $$\partial L/\partial b_1$$ | $$15\cdot1$$ | 15 |

PyTorch agrees on every number.

**Dead ReLU.** Change $$b_1$$ to $$-3$$. Now $$z=-1$$, $$h=0$$, $$\hat y=0$$, $$L=4$$. The ReLU derivative at $$z<0$$ is 0, so $$\partial L/\partial w_1=\partial L/\partial b_1=0$$, and $$\partial L/\partial w_2=2(0-2)\cdot h=0$$ as well. If a unit is negative for every input in the data, it never receives a gradient again. That is a "dead" ReLU.

sections.heading: Two gradients worth memorising
sections.body:
**Logistic loss.** For $$L=-\log\sigma(z)$$ with $$z=w\cdot x$$ (positive label), $$\frac{dL}{dz}=\sigma(z)-1$$, so

$$\nabla_wL=(\sigma(z)-1)\,x$$

With $$w=(0.5,-0.3)$$ and $$x=(1,2)$$: $$z=-0.1$$, $$\sigma(z)=0.47502$$, gradient $$=(-0.5250,-1.0500)$$. The sign is negative, so gradient *descent* increases $$w\cdot x$$, which pushes the predicted probability up toward the true label. Good sanity check.

**Softmax plus cross-entropy.** With logits $$o$$, probabilities $$p=\mathrm{softmax}(o)$$ and one-hot label $$y$$, the gradient of the cross-entropy with respect to the logits is

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial o}=p-y$$

"Prediction minus target." It is bounded in $$[-1,1]$$ per entry, which is part of why this pairing trains so well. It is also why PyTorch's `CrossEntropyLoss` takes raw logits and fuses the log-softmax internally.

sections.heading: Autograd behaviours that cause real bugs
sections.body:
**Gradients accumulate.** Calling `backward()` *adds* into `.grad`. It does not overwrite it.

```python
w = torch.tensor(1.0, requires_grad=True)
for _ in range(3):
    (2 * w).backward()
print(w.grad)   # tensor(6.)  not 2
```

That is why every training loop calls `optimizer.zero_grad()` each step. Forgetting it means each update uses the running sum of all past gradients. Deliberate accumulation over several micro-batches before one `optimizer.step()` is the legitimate use of the same behaviour (divide the loss by the number of micro-batches so the scale matches).

**Masking after the fact does not stop NaN gradients.** The PyTorch autograd notes warn that if a division by zero is recorded in the graph, autograd still differentiates through it even if you mask the result out afterwards:

```python
x = torch.tensor([0.0, 1.0], requires_grad=True)
y = torch.where(x > 0, 1 / x, torch.zeros_like(x))
y.sum().backward()
print(x.grad)   # tensor([nan, -1.])
```

The fix is to keep the bad operation out of the graph: make the denominator safe *before* dividing (for example compute on `torch.where(x > 0, x, torch.ones_like(x))`) and then select.

keyPoints: Chain rule: multiply local derivatives along a path; sum over paths when a variable fans out.
Backprop = forward pass that caches intermediates + reverse pass that multiplies upstream gradient by local derivative.
Reverse mode gives all parameter gradients of a scalar loss for a small constant multiple of the forward cost.
Logistic loss gradient: (σ(z) − y)x; softmax + cross-entropy gradient w.r.t. logits: p − y.
ReLU passes gradient 1 when active and 0 when inactive; units stuck negative stop learning.
PyTorch accumulates into .grad; call optimizer.zero_grad() every step unless you are accumulating on purpose.

gotchas.trap: Applying the chain rule but forgetting the inner derivative (e.g. answering 26 for d/dx (3x²+1)² at x=2).
gotchas.correct: Multiply by du/dx too: 26 × 12 = 312.

gotchas.trap: Masking NaN or inf results with torch.where and assuming the gradient is clean.
gotchas.correct: Autograd still differentiates the masked branch; make the input safe before the dangerous operation.

gotchas.trap: Applying softmax yourself and then passing probabilities to CrossEntropyLoss.
gotchas.correct: CrossEntropyLoss expects raw logits; it applies log-softmax internally.

lessons.lab:
1. Re-derive the tiny network gradients on paper, then build the same graph in PyTorch and compare every gradient.
2. Change `b1` to −3 and confirm the dead-ReLU gradients are zero.
3. Remove `optimizer.zero_grad()` from a small regression training loop and watch the loss; then add explicit gradient accumulation over 4 micro-batches and show it matches one big batch when the loss is divided by 4.
4. Reproduce the `torch.where` NaN gradient and fix it with a safe denominator.

lessons.title: Jacobians, Hessians and curvature
lessons.summary: Vector-valued derivatives, second derivatives and what curvature does to gradient descent: the 2/λ stability limit, condition numbers, classifying critical points and why Newton's method is not used for large models.

sections.heading: The Jacobian: derivatives of vector functions
sections.body:
For $$f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$$ the **Jacobian** is the $$m\times n$$ matrix $$J_{ij}=\partial f_i/\partial x_j$$: one row per output, one column per input. The linear model becomes $$f(x+\delta)\approx f(x)+J\delta$$, and the chain rule becomes matrix multiplication:

$$J_{g\circ f}(x)=J_g(f(x))\,J_f(x)$$

A classifier head mapping a 768-dimensional feature to 10 logits has a $$10\times768$$ Jacobian.

**Softmax Jacobian.** For $$s=\mathrm{softmax}(z)$$:

$$\frac{\partial s_i}{\partial z_j}=s_i(\delta_{ij}-s_j)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad J=\mathrm{diag}(s)-ss^\top$$

For $$z=(2,1,0.1)$$ this is a $$3\times3$$ matrix with diagonal $$\approx(0.225,0.184,0.089)$$ and negative off-diagonals. It is **symmetric**, and every row and column **sums to zero**: adding the same constant to all logits does not change the softmax, so the all-ones direction is in its null space, and the Jacobian is singular.

**Backprop never builds full Jacobians.** For a scalar loss it only needs vector-Jacobian products $$v^\top J$$, which can be computed without materialising $$J$$. That is what keeps reverse mode cheap.

sections.heading: The Hessian: curvature
sections.body:
For a scalar $$f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$$, the **Hessian** is the $$n\times n$$ matrix of second derivatives $$H_{ij}=\partial^2f/\partial x_i\partial x_j$$ (symmetric for smooth $$f$$). The second-order Taylor model is

$$f(x+\delta)\approx f(x)+\nabla f^\top\delta+\tfrac12\delta^\top H\delta$$

The eigenvectors of $$H$$ are the principal curvature directions and the eigenvalues are how sharply the surface bends along them. For $$f=x^2+3y^2$$, $$H=\mathrm{diag}(2,6)$$: the bowl is three times steeper in $$y$$ than in $$x$$.

**Condition number** $$\kappa=\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}$$ (here 3) measures how stretched the bowl is. Large $$\kappa$$ means ill-conditioning.

sections.heading: Curvature sets the maximum learning rate
sections.body:
On a quadratic, gradient descent along an eigen-direction with curvature $$\lambda$$ multiplies the error by $$(1-\eta\lambda)$$ each step. It converges only if $$|1-\eta\lambda|<1$$, that is

$$\eta<\frac{2}{\lambda_{\max}}$$

and the **largest** eigenvalue sets the limit.

- $$f=x^2$$ ($$\lambda=2$$), five steps from $$x=1$$: $$\eta=0.1\to0.32768$$ (smooth), $$\eta=0.9\to-0.32768$$ (oscillates, still converges), $$\eta=1.1\to-2.48832$$ (diverges).
- $$f=x^2+3y^2$$: limit $$2/6\approx0.333$$. With $$\eta=0.3$$ both coordinates shrink (factors 0.4 and 0.8). With $$\eta=0.34$$ the $$y$$ factor is $$|1-2.04|=1.04$$, so $$y$$ grows (about 2.19 after 20 steps) even though $$x$$ converges nicely.

The squeeze: $$\eta$$ must be small enough for the steepest direction, but then progress along the flattest direction runs at rate $$1-\eta\lambda_{\min}$$, which is slow when $$\kappa$$ is large. The visible symptom is **zig-zagging** across a narrow valley. Momentum and per-parameter adaptive methods (Adam) are practical answers.

sections.heading: Classifying critical points
sections.body:
At a critical point $$\nabla f=0$$. The Hessian's eigenvalues decide what it is:

| Hessian eigenvalues | Point |
|---|---|
| all $$>0$$ (positive definite) | local minimum |
| all $$<0$$ | local maximum |
| mixed signs | **saddle point** |
| some $$=0$$ | test is inconclusive |

$$f=x^2-y^2$$ has $$H=\mathrm{diag}(2,-2)$$ at the origin: a saddle. Downhill exists (along $$y$$) even though the gradient is zero there. In high-dimensional non-convex losses, critical points with a mix of signs are far more common than true local minima, so "gradient near zero" usually does not mean "at a minimum".

sections.heading: Newton's method and why LLMs do not use it
sections.body:
Minimising the quadratic model gives the **Newton step**

$$x\leftarrow x-H^{-1}\nabla f$$

On an exact quadratic it lands on the minimum in one step: from $$(1,1)$$ on $$x^2+3y^2$$, $$H^{-1}\nabla f=(1,1)$$, so the next point is $$(0,0)$$. It rescales every direction by its curvature, so ill-conditioning disappears.

Why it is not used to train large networks:

1. **Size.** $$H$$ has $$n^2$$ entries. For $$n=7\times10^9$$ that is about $$4.9\times10^{19}$$ numbers, far beyond any memory, and inversion costs $$O(n^3)$$.
2. **Saddles.** Newton's method jumps to *any* critical point of the quadratic model, including saddles, unless modified.
3. **Noise.** Mini-batch Hessian estimates are noisy.

Adam's division by $$\sqrt{\hat v}$$ can be read, as an intuition, as a cheap diagonal rescaling per parameter: a poor man's preconditioner.

```python
import torch
from torch.autograd.functional import jacobian, hessian
print(jacobian(lambda z: torch.softmax(z, 0), torch.tensor([2., 1., .1])).shape)  # (3, 3)
print(hessian(lambda v: v[0]**2 + 3*v[1]**2, torch.tensor([1., 1.])))             # diag(2, 6)
```

keyPoints: Jacobian of f: Rⁿ→Rᵐ is m×n (rows = outputs); chain rule = Jacobian product.
Softmax Jacobian = diag(s) − ssᵀ: symmetric, rows sum to zero, singular.
Hessian eigenvalues = curvature along principal directions; κ = λmax/λmin measures ill-conditioning.
Gradient descent on a quadratic is stable only if η < 2/λmax.
Zero gradient + mixed-sign Hessian eigenvalues = saddle point.
Newton's step −H⁻¹∇f solves a quadratic in one step but is infeasible at LLM scale (n² entries).

gotchas.correct: Convention is outputs × inputs: 10×768.

gotchas.trap: Picking a learning rate from the flattest direction of the loss.
gotchas.correct: Stability is set by the steepest curvature: η < 2/λmax.

gotchas.trap: Treating every zero-gradient point as a minimum.
gotchas.correct: Check the Hessian's eigenvalue signs; mixed signs mean a saddle.

lessons.title: Optimisers: SGD, momentum, Adam, AdamW and schedules
lessons.summary: How every common optimiser actually updates parameters, with verified numbers: mini-batch noise, the learning rate, momentum, Adam's bias correction, decoupled weight decay in AdamW, and warmup plus cosine schedules as used in real LLM recipes.

sections.heading: From gradient descent to mini-batch SGD
sections.body:
The training loss is an average over examples, $$L(\theta)=\frac1N\sum_i\ell_i(\theta)$$. Full-batch gradient descent uses the exact gradient: $$\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\nabla L(\theta)$$.

**Mini-batch SGD** uses the average gradient over a random batch of $$B$$ examples. It is an unbiased estimate of the full gradient, and its noise standard deviation shrinks like $$1/\sqrt B$$ (the standard error of a mean). In a simulation with per-example gradient std 2, the batch-mean std was 0.50 at $$B=16$$ and 0.25 at $$B=64$$: **4x the batch halves the noise**, it does not quarter it.

Vocabulary: one **step** (iteration) = one parameter update; one **epoch** = one pass over the data. Some noise is useful: it helps escape saddles and sharp regions.

sections.heading: The learning rate
sections.body:
The learning rate $$\eta$$ is the single most important hyperparameter. From the curvature lesson: on a quadratic, $$\eta<2/\lambda_{\max}$$ or training diverges. Practical reading of a loss curve:

- Loss decreasing very slowly and smoothly: $$\eta$$ probably too small.
- Loss oscillating or jumping up, or NaN: $$\eta$$ too large (or a numerical problem).

Five steps on $$f=x^2$$ from $$x=1$$: $$\eta=0.1\to0.328$$, $$\eta=0.9\to-0.328$$ (oscillates), $$\eta=1.1\to-2.488$$ (diverges).

sections.heading: Momentum
sections.body:
PyTorch's `SGD` with momentum $$\mu$$ (dampening 0) keeps a buffer:

$$b_t=\mu b_{t-1}+g_t,\qquad\theta_t=\theta_{t-1}-\eta\,b_t$$

(the first step sets $$b_1=g_1$$). The buffer is a running sum of past gradients with geometric decay.

- **Consistent directions accelerate.** With a constant gradient the step grows toward $$\eta g/(1-\mu)$$. With $$\mu=0.9$$, $$\eta=0.1$$, $$g=1$$: steps of 0.1, 0.19, … approaching 1.0, which is 10x plain SGD.
- **Oscillating directions cancel.** In a zig-zagging valley the across-valley components alternate in sign and partly cancel, while the along-valley components add up.

PyTorch notes that its formulation puts the learning rate outside the buffer, which differs subtly from some papers. `nesterov=True` uses a look-ahead variant.

sections.heading: Adam: per-parameter adaptive steps
sections.body:
Adam keeps exponential moving averages of the gradient and of its square:

$$m_t=\beta_1m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)g_t,\qquad v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)g_t^2$$

Because $$m_0=v_0=0$$, early averages are biased toward zero, so Adam **bias-corrects** them:

$$\hat m_t=\frac{m_t}{1-\beta_1^t},\qquad\hat v_t=\frac{v_t}{1-\beta_2^t},\qquad\theta_t=\theta_{t-1}-\eta\frac{\hat m_t}{\sqrt{\hat v_t}+\epsilon}$$

**Consequences you can verify:**

- On step 1, $$\hat m_1=g$$ and $$\hat v_1=g^2$$, so the step is about $$\eta\,\mathrm{sign}(g)$$ **whatever the gradient's size**. With $$\eta=0.1$$ a parameter at 1.0 moves to 0.9 whether $$g=123$$ or $$g=0.001$$.
- Without bias correction, step 1 would be $$\eta\cdot\frac{0.1g}{\sqrt{0.001g^2}}\approx3.16\eta$$: an oversized first step.
- Step size is roughly scale-invariant per parameter: rarely updated or small-gradient parameters still move.

PyTorch 2.8 defaults: `Adam(lr=0.001, betas=(0.9, 0.999), eps=1e-08, weight_decay=0)`.

sections.heading: Weight decay, L2 and AdamW
sections.body:
For plain SGD, adding an L2 penalty $$\frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2$$ to the loss is equivalent (after rescaling) to shrinking weights each step. **For Adam it is not** (Loshchilov & Hutter). The L2 term $$\lambda\theta$$ is added to the gradient, so it flows into $$m$$ and $$v$$ and is then divided by $$\sqrt{\hat v}$$; the effective decay depends on each parameter's gradient history.

**AdamW decouples** the decay and applies it directly to the weights:

$$\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\lambda\theta$$

The PyTorch docs say weight decay "does not accumulate in the momentum nor variance." With zero gradient, $$\eta=0.1$$ and $$\lambda=0.01$$, a weight goes from 1.0 to 0.999 in one step.

A 100-step experiment ($$\eta=0.01$$, $$\lambda=0.1$$, zero task gradient on that weight): coupled L2 in Adam shrank it from 1.0 to about 0.22, because Adam normalised the tiny decay gradient into full-size steps; decoupled decay shrank it to $$0.999^{100}\approx0.905$$, exactly as the formula predicts.

PyTorch 2.8 specifics (check the version you run):

- `AdamW` default `weight_decay=0.01`; `Adam` default `weight_decay=0`.
- `Adam(weight_decay=…)` is coupled L2 **unless** `decoupled_weight_decay=True`, which makes it behave like AdamW.

sections.heading: Schedules and warmup
sections.body:
The learning rate usually changes over training.

**Transformer (2017) schedule:** $$\eta=d_{model}^{-0.5}\min(\text{step}^{-0.5},\ \text{step}\cdot\text{warmup}^{-1.5})$$ with warmup = 4000. It rises linearly, peaks at step 4000 (about $$6.99\times10^{-4}$$ for $$d_{model}=512$$) and then decays as $$1/\sqrt{\text{step}}$$, halving by step 16000. The paper used Adam with $$\beta_2=0.98$$ and $$\epsilon=10^{-9}$$.

**Llama 2 recipe (Sec. 2.2):** AdamW with $$\beta_1=0.9$$, $$\beta_2=0.95$$, eps $$10^{-5}$$; cosine schedule with 2000 warmup steps decaying to 10% of peak (peak $$3\times10^{-4}$$ for 7B/13B, so the final value is $$3\times10^{-5}$$); weight decay 0.1; gradient clipping 1.0.

**Why warmup.** At the start, weights are random, gradients can be large and Adam's second-moment estimates are based on very few samples. A short ramp avoids large destabilising early updates. (This is the common practical explanation.)

```python
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4, betas=(0.9, 0.95), weight_decay=0.1)
warm = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LinearLR(opt, start_factor=0.01, total_iters=2000)
cos  = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(opt, T_max=total - 2000, eta_min=3e-5)
sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.SequentialLR(opt, [warm, cos], milestones=[2000])
for batch in loader:
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = model(batch).loss
    loss.backward()
    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
    opt.step()
    sched.step()          # after opt.step()
```

PyTorch warns that calling `scheduler.step()` **before** `optimizer.step()` skips the first value of the schedule.

keyPoints: Mini-batch gradient noise std scales as 1/√B: 4x batch halves the noise.
PyTorch momentum: b ← μb + g, θ ← θ − ηb; constant gradient gives steps approaching ηg/(1−μ).
Adam bias-corrects m and v; the first step is about η per parameter regardless of gradient size.
L2 in Adam ≠ weight decay; AdamW applies θ ← θ − ηλθ directly, outside the moments.
PyTorch 2.8: AdamW weight_decay defaults to 0.01, Adam to 0; Adam(decoupled_weight_decay=True) behaves like AdamW.
Llama 2: AdamW (0.9, 0.95), cosine to 10% of peak, 2000 warmup steps, wd 0.1, clip 1.0.
Call scheduler.step() after optimizer.step().

gotchas.trap: Using torch.optim.Adam(weight_decay=0.1) and believing it is AdamW.
gotchas.correct: It adds λθ to the gradient (coupled L2) unless decoupled_weight_decay=True; use AdamW for decoupled decay.

gotchas.trap: Expecting a 4x larger batch to cut gradient noise by 4x.
gotchas.correct: Noise std scales with 1/√B, so it halves.

gotchas.trap: Expecting Adam's first update to be proportional to the gradient.
gotchas.correct: Bias correction makes step 1 about lr in size for every parameter with nonzero gradient.

lessons.title: Loss landscapes: convexity, saddles and unstable gradients
lessons.summary: Convex versus non-convex losses, why saddle points matter more than local minima in high dimensions, the multiplication that makes gradients vanish or explode, and the remedies: activations, initialisation, residual paths and gradient clipping.

sections.heading: Convexity: when local equals global
sections.body:
A function is **convex** if the chord between any two points lies on or above the graph:

$$f(\lambda a+(1-\lambda)b)\le\lambda f(a)+(1-\lambda)f(b),\quad\lambda\in[0,1]$$

For twice-differentiable $$f$$, convexity is equivalent to the Hessian being positive semidefinite everywhere. The payoff: **every local minimum of a convex function is a global minimum**, so a gradient method with a suitable step size cannot get trapped.

Convex in the parameters: least-squares linear regression, logistic regression's negative log-likelihood. **Not convex:** essentially any neural network with a hidden layer. One easy argument: permuting the hidden units of a layer gives a different parameter vector with the same loss, so minima come in many equivalent copies, and the average of two such copies is generally worse, which violates convexity.

Convexity does **not** make any learning rate safe: the $$\eta<2/\lambda_{\max}$$ limit still applies.

sections.heading: Local minima, saddle points and plateaus
sections.body:
In non-convex losses three kinds of places slow training down:

- **Local minima** that are worse than the best one.
- **Saddle points**: zero gradient but downhill directions exist (Hessian has negative eigenvalues).
- **Plateaus**: wide flat regions with tiny gradients.

In high dimensions, a critical point is a local minimum only if *every* one of millions of curvature directions curves upward. Saddle points with mixed curvature are therefore much more common than local minima, and much of the "stuck" behaviour in deep learning is near saddles or on plateaus rather than in bad minima. Plain gradient descent slows near a saddle because the gradient is small, but mini-batch noise and momentum help push the iterate off it.

Diagnostic: a loss that plateaus with a tiny gradient norm and then suddenly drops again is the classic saddle or plateau signature.

sections.heading: Vanishing and exploding gradients
sections.body:
Backprop through $$L$$ layers multiplies $$L$$ Jacobians:

$$\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial h_0}=\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial h_L}\,J_L J_{L-1}\cdots J_1$$

A product of many factors either shrinks or grows geometrically:

- Sigmoid derivatives are at most 0.25, so across ten sigmoid layers the activation derivatives alone multiply the gradient by at most $0.25^{10}\approx9.5\times10^{-7}$. Early layers stop learning: **vanishing**.
- Per-layer factor 0.9 for 50 layers gives $$0.9^{50}\approx0.005$$; factor 1.1 gives $$1.1^{50}\approx117$$: **exploding**.

Pascanu et al. analyse this for recurrent networks, where the same weight matrix is multiplied in at every time step, and tie it to the size of that matrix: a largest singular value below 1 (scaled by a bound on the activation derivative) is sufficient for vanishing, and above 1 is necessary for exploding; in the linear case the spectral radius plays this role.

**Remedies, each tied to the maths:**

| Remedy | What it does to the product |
|---|---|
| ReLU-family activations | derivative 1 on the active side instead of at most 0.25 |
| Careful initialisation (He: variance $$2/\text{fan-in}$$ for ReLU) | keeps each layer's signal and gradient variance near 1 |
| Residual connections $$h_{l+1}=h_l+F(h_l)$$ | Jacobian is $$I+\partial F/\partial h$$, an identity path that does not shrink |
| Normalisation (LayerNorm, RMSNorm) | keeps activations at a controlled scale |
| Gradient clipping | caps the size of an exploding update (does not fix vanishing) |

sections.heading: Gradient clipping in practice
sections.body:
**Clip by global norm** (the usual choice):

$$g\leftarrow g\cdot\min\Big(1,\frac{c}{\|g\|}\Big)$$

where $$\|g\|$$ is the norm of **all** parameter gradients concatenated into one vector. The direction is preserved; only the length is capped.

PyTorch: `clip_grad_norm_(parameters, max_norm, norm_type=2.0, error_if_nonfinite=False, foreach=None)` returns the **total norm before clipping**. If parameter A has gradient 3 and B has gradient 4, the global norm is 5; with `max_norm=1.0` the call returns 5.0 and the gradients become 0.6 and 0.8.

**Clip by value** (`clip_grad_value_`) clamps each element independently to $$[-c,c]$$. The same (3, 4) with $$c=1$$ becomes (1, 1): the direction changes. That is why norm clipping is the default for transformers (Llama 2 uses a norm of 1.0).

Log the returned norm every step. Spikes in the gradient norm often precede loss spikes and NaNs and are one of the most useful health signals in LLM training.

sections.heading: A debugging checklist for unstable training
sections.body:
When loss spikes or goes NaN:

1. **Plot the global gradient norm** (from `clip_grad_norm_`). Spikes point to exploding updates.
2. **Check the learning rate and warmup.** Too high a peak or no warmup is the most common cause.
3. **Enable or lower norm clipping** (1.0 is a common starting point).
4. **Look for numerical hazards**: `log(0)`, division by zero in a masked branch, softmax without max-subtraction, fp16 overflow.
5. **Check initialisation and normalisation placement** if gradients vanish in early layers.

Fix the cause before reaching for a smaller learning rate everywhere: an unnecessarily small $$\eta$$ just makes training slow.

keyPoints: Convex: chord above graph; Hessian PSD everywhere; every local minimum is global.
Linear and logistic regression losses are convex in the weights; neural networks are not.
In high dimensions saddle points and plateaus are more common obstacles than bad local minima.
Backprop multiplies per-layer Jacobians, so gradients shrink or grow geometrically with depth.
Remedies: ReLU-family activations, He initialisation, residual paths, normalisation, norm clipping.
clip_grad_norm_ uses the global norm over all parameters and returns the pre-clip norm; clip_grad_value_ clamps elementwise and changes direction.

gotchas.trap: Using gradient clipping to fix vanishing gradients.
gotchas.correct: Clipping only caps large gradients; vanishing needs activation, initialisation or architecture changes.

gotchas.trap: Assuming clip_grad_norm_ clips each parameter tensor separately.
gotchas.correct: It computes one norm over all parameters together and scales them all by the same factor.

gotchas.trap: Concluding training is at a minimum because the gradient norm is near zero.
gotchas.correct: It may be a saddle or plateau; check whether the loss later drops or probe the curvature.

2. Add residual connections to the sigmoid model and repeat.
3. Set gradients (3, 4) on two parameters and compare `clip_grad_norm_` and `clip_grad_value_` with threshold 1.0.
4. Train a small model with a deliberately too-high learning rate, log the returned gradient norm each step, and show that clipping at 1.0 stabilises it.

lessons.title: Random variables, distributions, expectation and variance
lessons.summary: Build the vocabulary every ML paper assumes: random variables, the Bernoulli, categorical and Gaussian distributions, and the algebra of expectation and variance, plus the variance convention traps in NumPy, pandas and PyTorch.

sections.heading: Random variables: numbers attached to outcomes
sections.body:
A **random variable** $$X$$ maps each outcome of an experiment to a number. A **discrete** variable has a probability mass function (PMF) $$P(X=x)$$ that sums to 1. A **continuous** variable has a probability density function (PDF) $$p(x)$$ that integrates to 1.

A density is *not* a probability: $$p(x)$$ can exceed 1 (a Gaussian with $$\sigma=0.1$$ peaks near 4). Only areas under it, $$P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^b p(x)\,dx$$, are probabilities.

In ML you meet random variables everywhere: a per-item eval score (0 or 1), the next token an LLM samples, the noise in a regression target, a mini-batch gradient, the initial value of a weight.

sections.heading: The three distributions you must know cold
sections.body:
| Distribution | Support | Parameters | Mean | Variance | Where it shows up |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bernoulli($$p$$) | {0, 1} | $$p$$ | $$p$$ | $$p(1-p)$$ | one eval item right/wrong, a binary label |
| Categorical($$\pi_1..\pi_K$$) | {1..K} | $$K$$ probabilities summing to 1 ($$K-1$$ free) | — | — | next-token prediction over a vocabulary |
| Gaussian $$\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$$ | all reals | $$\mu,\sigma^2$$ | $$\mu$$ | $$\sigma^2$$ | weight init, regression noise, CLT limit |

- A **binomial** count is the sum of $$n$$ independent Bernoullis: mean $$np$$, variance $$np(1-p)$$.
- A categorical variable is often written as a **one-hot** vector; then $$E[\text{one-hot}]=\pi$$, the probability vector itself. A softmax layer outputs exactly such a $$\pi$$.
- For a Gaussian, about **68.3% / 95.4% / 99.7%** of mass lies within 1 / 2 / 3 standard deviations, and the two-sided 95% point is $$z\approx1.96$$.

sections.heading: Expectation: linear, always
sections.body:
$$E[X]=\sum_x x\,P(X=x)$$ (or $$\int x\,p(x)\,dx$$). A fair die has $$E[X]=3.5$$, a value it can never show.

**Linearity** holds with *no* independence assumption:
$$E[aX+bY+c]=aE[X]+bE[Y]+c$$

So the expected number of correct answers on $$n$$ items with per-item accuracies $$p_i$$ is $$\sum p_i$$, even if the items are correlated. In general $$E[f(X)]\neq f(E[X])$$ unless $$f$$ is linear (Jensen's inequality covers convex $$f$$).

sections.heading: Variance and covariance
sections.body:
$$\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[(X-\mu)^2]=E[X^2]-\mu^2$$, and the standard deviation is $$\sigma=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)}$$, in the same units as $$X$$.

- $$\mathrm{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\mathrm{Var}(X)$$: shifting does nothing, scaling squares.
- $$\mathrm{Var}(X+Y)=\mathrm{Var}(X)+\mathrm{Var}(Y)+2\,\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)$$.
- If $$X,Y$$ are independent, $$\mathrm{Cov}=0$$, so $$\mathrm{Var}(X\pm Y)=\mathrm{Var}(X)+\mathrm{Var}(Y)$$. Variances **add even when you subtract**.
- The mean of $$n$$ i.i.d. variables has variance $$\sigma^2/n$$. This one line is the root of standard errors, mini-batch gradient noise and why bigger evals are more trustworthy.

Zero covariance does **not** imply independence (take $$X$$ symmetric around 0 and $$Y=X^2$$).

sections.heading: Sample variance in code: the ddof trap
sections.body:
Dividing by $$n$$ gives the maximum-likelihood (biased) estimate; dividing by $$n-1$$ (Bessel's correction) gives the unbiased one. Libraries disagree on the default:

| Call on [1, 2, 3, 4] | Divisor | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `np.var(x)` | $$n$$ (`ddof=0`) | 1.25 |
| `pd.Series(x).var()` | $$n-1$$ (`ddof=1`) | 1.6667 |
| `torch.var(t)` | $$n-1$$ (`correction=1`) | 1.6667 |
| `statistics.variance(x)` | $$n-1$$ | 1.6667 |
| `statistics.pvariance(x)` | $$n$$ | 1.25 |

When a port from NumPy to PyTorch "almost" matches, check this first. LayerNorm, by contrast, normalises with the biased (divide-by-$$n$$) variance.

keyPoints: Bernoulli($$p$$): mean $$p$$, variance $$p(1-p)$$, maximised at $$p=0.5$$.
A categorical distribution over K classes has K probabilities summing to 1; softmax outputs one.
Linearity of expectation needs no independence; additivity of variance does.
$$\mathrm{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\mathrm{Var}(X)$$ and the variance of a mean of n i.i.d. draws is $$\sigma^2/n$$.
np.var defaults to ddof=0; pandas .var() and torch.var default to dividing by n-1.

gotchas.trap: A density value above 1 is a bug.
gotchas.correct: Densities can exceed 1; only integrals over intervals must lie in [0, 1].

gotchas.trap: $$\mathrm{Var}(X-Y)=\mathrm{Var}(X)-\mathrm{Var}(Y)$$.
gotchas.correct: For independent X, Y it is $$\mathrm{Var}(X)+\mathrm{Var}(Y)$$; subtracting noisy quantities adds noise.

gotchas.trap: Uncorrelated means independent.
gotchas.correct: Zero covariance only rules out linear dependence; Y = X squared is uncorrelated with a symmetric X yet fully dependent.

gotchas.trap: np.var and torch.var compute the same thing.
gotchas.correct: np.var divides by n by default, torch.var by n-1 (correction=1).

lessons.lab:
Run this on the course runner (Python 3.9, NumPy 2.0, PyTorch 2.8). Predict each printed line before you run it.

~~~python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, torch

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
scores = rng.binomial(1, 0.8, size=100_000)       # Bernoulli(0.8) per-item eval scores
print(round(float(scores.mean()), 3), round(float(scores.var()), 3))   # close to p=0.8 and p(1-p)=0.16

die = np.arange(1, 7)
print(float(die.mean()), round(float(die.var()), 4))   # E = 3.5, Var = 35/12

x = [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(float(np.var(x)), round(float(pd.Series(x).var()), 4),
      round(torch.var(torch.tensor(x, dtype=torch.float32)).item(), 4))   # ddof 0 vs 1 vs 1
~~~

Expected output: `0.802 0.159`, then `3.5 2.9167`, then `1.25 1.6667 1.6667`. Now change `p` to 0.5 and confirm the variance rises to about 0.25, the Bernoulli maximum.

lessons.title: Conditional probability, independence and Bayes with base rates
lessons.summary: Learn to reason about P(A | B) precisely, tell independence from conditional independence, and apply Bayes' theorem so that base rates never fool you about classifiers, LLM judges or safety filters.

sections.heading: Conditional probability and the product rule
sections.body:
$$P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$$ for $$P(B)>0$$. Read it as: restrict the world to cases where $$B$$ happened, then ask how often $$A$$ also happened.

Rearranged, this is the **product rule** $$P(A\cap B)=P(A\mid B)P(B)$$, and summing over a partition gives the **law of total probability**:
$$P(A)=\sum_i P(A\mid B_i)P(B_i)$$

An autoregressive LLM is the product rule applied repeatedly: $$p(x_1..x_T)=\prod_t p(x_t\mid x_{<t})$$.

sections.heading: Independence vs conditional independence
sections.body:
- **Independent:** $$P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$$, equivalently $$P(A\mid B)=P(A)$$. Knowing $$B$$ tells you nothing about $$A$$.
- **Mutually exclusive** is a different idea: $$P(A\cap B)=0$$. Two exclusive events with positive probability are maximally *dependent*.
- **Conditionally independent given C:** $$P(A\cap B\mid C)=P(A\mid C)P(B\mid C)$$. Naive Bayes assumes features are conditionally independent given the class. That does *not* make them marginally independent: two symptoms of the same disease are correlated in the population precisely because both depend on the disease.

Inclusion-exclusion links the pieces: $$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$$.

sections.heading: Bayes' theorem
sections.body:
$$P(H\mid E)=\frac{P(E\mid H)\,P(H)}{P(E)}=\frac{P(E\mid H)P(H)}{P(E\mid H)P(H)+P(E\mid\neg H)P(\neg H)}$$

- $$P(H)$$ is the **prior** (base rate, prevalence).
- $$P(E\mid H)$$ is the **likelihood**; for a test, sensitivity (recall, true-positive rate).
- $$P(E\mid\neg H)$$ is the false-positive rate (1 − specificity).
- $$P(H\mid E)$$ is the **posterior**; for a classifier, the precision (positive predictive value).

sections.heading: Base rates: the worked example you should be able to do in your head
sections.body:
A detector flags 1% prevalence content with 99% sensitivity and a 5% false-positive rate. Think in **natural frequencies** over 10,000 items:

- 100 are truly positive; 99 of them are flagged.
- 9,900 are negative; 5% of them, 495, are flagged anyway.
- Flags total 594, of which 99 are real: $$99/594\approx0.1667$$.

A "99% accurate" detector is right only **one time in six** when it fires, because negatives vastly outnumber positives. At 10% prevalence the same detector gives 0.6875. A second, conditionally independent positive updates 0.1667 to about 0.798: yesterday's posterior is today's prior.

This is exactly the situation of an LLM judge, toxicity filter or fraud model on rare events: always ask for the base rate before interpreting a flag.

keyPoints: $$P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)$$; the product rule chains these, which is how autoregressive LMs factorise a sequence.
Independent means P(A and B) = P(A)P(B); mutually exclusive events with positive probability are dependent.
Conditional independence given a cause does not imply marginal independence.
Posterior = likelihood x prior / evidence; with rare positives most flags are false positives.
Natural frequencies (counts out of 10,000) make base-rate problems hard to get wrong.

gotchas.trap: $$P(\text{positive}\mid\text{toxic})=0.99$$, so a flagged item is 99% likely toxic.
gotchas.correct: That confuses $$P(E\mid H)$$ with $$P(H\mid E)$$; at 1% prevalence and 5% FPR the posterior is about 17%.

gotchas.trap: Mutually exclusive and independent mean the same thing.
gotchas.correct: Exclusive events cannot co-occur, so learning one happened changes the other to zero: they are dependent.

gotchas.trap: Naive Bayes features must be uncorrelated in the data.
gotchas.correct: Naive Bayes assumes independence given the class; features can be strongly correlated overall.

lessons.lab:
Write the posterior as a function and reproduce the natural-frequency table.

~~~python
def posterior(prior, sens, fpr):
    """P(condition | positive) from Bayes' theorem."""
    evidence = sens * prior + fpr * (1 - prior)
    return sens * prior / evidence

p1 = posterior(0.01, 0.99, 0.05)
print(round(p1, 4))                      # one positive test
print(round(posterior(p1, 0.99, 0.05), 4))   # second, conditionally independent positive
print(round(posterior(0.10, 0.99, 0.05), 4)) # same test, 10% prevalence

# Natural frequencies: 10,000 items
n = 10_000; sick = n * 0.01
tp = sick * 0.99; fp = (n - sick) * 0.05
print(int(tp), int(fp), round(tp / (tp + fp), 4))
~~~

Expected output: `0.1667`, `0.7984`, `0.6875`, then `99 495 0.1667`. Extend it: find the false-positive rate needed for a flag to be 90% reliable at 1% prevalence.
